1. There is broad agreement between the parties, as to how this
appeal can be disposed off and hence, we notice only the skeletal
facts which led to the impugned order.
2.  The Corporate Debtor (CD) was admitted  to  the Corporate
Insolvency  Resolution  Process  (CIRP)  on  24.04.2017,  on  an
application filed by an operational creditor. The appellant herein is
an ex-Director of the CD who resigned in the year 2006 but the fact
remains that the CD had taken a loan from the ICICI Bank Ltd. to
purchase an asset located at Plot No.C-158, Sector 41, Noida, Uttar
Pradesh, which was registered in the name of the appellant. The
Resolution  Professional  (RP),  though  found  the  claim  of  the
operational  creditor  to  be  invalid,  recommended  liquidation
proceedings, especially since the whereabouts of the CD remained
elusive. 
3. The RP was appointed as the Liquidator and when proceedings
were taken against the property, the appellant agreed to proffer a

--- Page 276 ---
2
proposal  to  settle  the  dues  of  the  Employees  Provident  Funds
Organization  (EPFO),  Income  T ax  Department,  Employee’s  State
Insurance  Corporation  (ESIC)  and  the  Goods  and  Services  T ax
Department (GST). The proposal did not meet the approval of the
GST Department whose total dues with interest comes to more than
Rs.8  crores.  The  appellant  while  submitting  the  proposal  also
undertook  that  he  would  surrender   vacant  possession  of  the
property if the proposal was not accepted. Repeated proposals were
made but rejected by the GST Department. The appellant has also
raised a contention that the appeal against the demand made by
the GST Department is pending consideration with a stay, on pre-
deposit having been made. 
4. Dr.Menaka Guruswamy, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the appellant would submit that the property now sought to be sold
in  auction  is  the  only  residential  property  of  the  appellant.  The
appellant is ready to pay the market value of the property and to
that  end  produces  a  sale  deed  by  an  additional  affidavit  dated
22.07.2026  as  Annexure  A1.   The  sale  deed  is  said  to  be  of  a
comparable extent lying just adjacent to the subject property which
the Liquidator is proposing to sell in auction. 
5. The learned Counsel for the GST Department submits that the
valuation shown in the deed, now produced is Rs.2,25,000/-  which is

--- Page 277 ---
3
far lower than the market value as assessed by a valuer and is
astronomically  lesser  than  the  total  dues  of  the  CD  to  the  GST
Department. 
6. Learned Counsel appearing for the Liquidator points out that
the reserve price is far greater than that shown in the document
produced as Annexure A1. It is also submitted that as of now there is
no other property or asset of the CD identified by the Liquidator. 
7. Admittedly, the amounts due to the other departments namely,
the EPFO, ESIC and the Income T ax Department have been settled
as of now. Since no other properties of the CD have been identified,
it is only proper that the Liquidator be allowed to put the property
for  auction; the  offer  of the appellant being  not feasible.  In  the
auction  conducted  the  appellant  herein  would  be  entitled  to
participate in the auction and if there is a bid made higher to that
made by the appellant, the appellant would have the first refusal on
the higher bid and in the circumstance of undertaking to deposit the
higher bid amount and so depositing, the auction would be settled in
his favour.  In  the circumstances of the appellant purchasing  the
property, we make it clear that the dues of the GST Department
which  remain,  after  setting  of  the  auction  amounts  cannot  be
recovered by proceeding against the same property; merely because
it belongs to an erstwhile Director of the CD. We make it clear that

4

there is still balance demand necessarily it will have to be recovered
from the properties of the CD, if any identified.

--- Page 282 ---
1. We  have  heard  Mr.  Ravi  Prakash  Mehrotra,  learned
senior  counsel  and  Mr.  Joy  Basu,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the three appellants.
2. Respondents are not called upon to answer.
3. These appeals are directed against the judgment and
order dated 31st January, 2012 passed by the Division Bench
of the High Court of Allahabad, dismissing the Letters Patent
Appeals which were carried by the appellants from the orders
of dismissal of their respective writ petitions by the Single
Judge. 
4. What is not in dispute is that even before occurrence of
a vacancy on a substantive post, advertisement was issued.
Not only was this an impermissible course of action because
an existing  vacancy could  only  be  advertised and not  an
anticipated  vacancy,  advertisement  was  published  in  only
one newspaper whereas the requirement was publication in
two newspapers.
5. That apart, the process of recruitment could have been
set  in  motion  by  the  College,  where  the  appellants  were
appointed,  only  if  the  relevant  Commission  faltered  in
recommending  candidates  for  appointment  on  substantive
vacancies  which  were  reported.  Here,  no  such  situation
2

--- Page 283 ---
existed.
6. Reference  has  been  made  by  both  learned  senior
counsel  to  the  Removal  of  Difficulties  Order,  19811,  as
amended. The Order provided modalities to be followed if
vacancies, which are reported, remain unfilled for quite some
time. We see no reason to accept the submission based on
the  Order  because  there  was  no  difficulty  here  as  such
requiring  removal.  The  difficulty  was  the  College’s  self-
creation, which did not call for application of the Order. 
7. The Single Judge as well as the Division Bench of the
High Court appear to be right in their conclusions that there
has been total non-compliance of the provisions contained in
the Uttar Pradesh Secondary Education Services Commission
and Selection Boards Act, 1982 in appointing the appellants.
8. In terms of interim orders passed on the writ petitions
of the appellants, the respondent-State has paid them their
salary  till  they  retired  on  attaining  the  age  of
superannuation.  Appellants  must  consider  themselves
fortunate that the High Court did not direct recovery of any
amount from them having regard to the illegality touching
their  appointments.  A  party  cannot  be  worse-off  for
preferring an appeal; hence, we do not direct any recovery.
9. For  the  foregoing  reasons,  the  civil  appeals  are
1  Order
3

dismissed.

been convicted for the offences punishable under

--- Page 318 ---

BALAMANIAN                                         Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
M. GAGAN BOTHRA & ORS.                             Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. The  petitioner  seeks  initiation  of
contempt proceedings against the respondents
for flouting the order of this Court dated
30.10.2025 in SLP (C) No.31018/2025 (M. Gagan
Bothra  &  Ors.  v.  Balamanian),  which  is
reproduced below:
“1) After hearing learned counsel
for  the  petitioners,  we  see  no
reason and ground to entertain this
special leave petition.
2) At this stage learned counsel for
the petitioner prays for time to
vacate the suit premises. In the
facts and circumstances, we grant
time to vacate the suit property up
to 30.04.2026, subject to payment of
arrears of rent within one month and
regular  rent  on  month-to-month
1

--- Page 323 ---
basis.  It  is  directed  that  the
petitioners  shall  hand  over  the
peaceful vacant possession of the
premises to the respondent on or
before 30.04.2026 and shall not part
with or create third party right
therein. A usual undertaking shall
be filed within a period of three
weeks  from  today  before  the
Registrar  (Judicial),  Madras  High
Court. Non-filing of the undertaking
shall give a cause to the landlord
to execute the decree and the time
for  vacation  as  specified  above
shall not have any bearing to the
execution proceedings. Defiance of
the above terms, if any, may be
treated  as  non-compliance  of  the
order of this Court.
3) The Special Leave Petition is,
accordingly,  dismissed  with  above
terms.  Pending  application(s),  if
any, shall stand disposed of.
4) Ordered accordingly.”
3. The respondents were the SLP petitioners
and, therefore, to obtain the benefit of this
Court’s  order,  were  required  to  file  usual
undertaking before the Registrar concerned of
the High Court. The respondents submitted an
affidavit stating therein that there are no
arrears of rent due according to them because
the decree-holder is already having a sum of
Rs.6 crore, and for payment of rental arrears,
a Suit, namely, O.S. No. 514/2020, is pending
2

--- Page 324 ---
which is being contested.
4. The  submission  on  behalf  of  the
petitioner(s)  is  that  the  execution  of  the
decree got delayed because of the affidavit
filed  by  the  contemnor(s)/opposite  parties;
therefore, as this Court’s order was specific
that the SLP petitioner(s) shall be allowed to
stay in the premises up to 30.04.2026 subject
to payment of arrears, the opposite party has
violated the orders of this Court.
5. We are afraid, the aforesaid submission
is misconceived. This Court had not adjudicated
upon as to what amount was payable. This Court
had merely granted time to vacate subject to
payment of arrears. There is no dispute that in
the  execution  proceedings,  the  SLP
petitioner(s)  (i.e.,  contemnor(s)/  opposite
parties) have been evicted, and possession has
been obtained by the decree-holder. Besides,
there  is  no  admission  by  the  contemnor(s)/
opposite parties regarding any amount being due
and payable towards arrears of rent. Thus, in
absence of any specific adjudication by this
Court regarding payment of the arrears, we do
3

--- Page 325 ---
not find a case for initiation of contempt
proceedings against the opposite parties. The
contempt petition is, accordingly, dismissed.
6. We make it clear that dismissal of this
contempt  petition  shall  not  prejudice  the
rights of the parties in the pending suit or
any other proceeding inter se parties.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order  dated
19.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature
at Allahabad rejecting the regular bail prayer of
the appellant in connection with FIR No.379 of
2025  registered  at  P.S.  Karchhana,  District
Prayagraj.
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is
that in all there were seven accused; four co-
accused have been granted bail. 
Crl.A. No.@ SLP (Crl.) No.9494 of 2026                                             1

--- Page 333 ---
5. The bail prayer of the appellant is seemingly
rejected on the ground that he happens to be in
the police force. It has been submitted that the
role  attributed  to  the  appellant  is  no  way
different  from  the  one  attributed  to  other
accused.  Besides, it appears to be case of road
rage.  It has also been submitted that co-accused
Dinesh, who is the owner of Scorpio vehicle and
attributed the role of assaulting the deceased,
has been admitted to bail.
6. The learned counsel for the State has opposed
the  prayer  for  bail  on  the  ground  that  the
appellant being a member of police force ought to
have prevented such an incident.
7. Be that as it may, having regard to the
commonality of the allegations ascribed to the
accused, taking into account that other accused
have been admitted to bail, we are of the view
that the appellant is also entitled to be released
on bail pending trial.
8. The appeal, is accordingly, allowed.  The
Crl.A. No.@ SLP (Crl.) No.9494 of 2026                                             2

impugned order passed by the High Court rejecting
the bail prayer of the appellant stands set aside.

of the case.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

Non-Reportable 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No..............of 2026
[ @ Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.2163 of 2026 ]
Archana Avinash Shelke
....Appellant
Versus
State of Maharashtra and Anr.
....Respondents
O R D E R 
Leave granted. 
2. It  is  commonplace,  nay  customary  that  in-laws  are
dragged in to settle scores in cases arising out of marital
discord and often children are used to vilify each other. But
we  are  shocked  by  the  allegations  raised  herein  by  the
divorced mother that her son is constantly molested sexually
by his paternal aunt. The FIR is alleged to be a counterblast
to  an  FIR  lodged  by  the  divorced  father  with  an  equally
shocking allegation against the maternal uncle, here alleging
the offence against the twin sister of the boy. 
3. The appellant herein is the paternal aunt of the twins
born in the wedlock of her brother, who is now divorced. The
Page 1 of 5

--- Page 343 ---
decree of divorce, obtained on mutual consent is produced
as Annexure P1; dated 05.09.2023. The children are under
the  custody  of  the  father  with  visitation  rights  to  the
mother’s  home.  We  see  from  the  FIR  that  the  de-facto
complainant/mother  alleges  that  the  complaint  of  sexual
harassment was raised by her son even while she was in the
matrimonial home and she also spoke of having witnessed
one such incident. The entreaties to the husband did not
evoke any  response is the allegation. Obviously,  no such
allegation was raised even at the time of divorce nor was a
complaint  raised  at  any  time  before  the  FIR  filed  on
17.03.2024,  just  a  few  hours  after  the  father  filed  an
identical FIR. The FIS, on a plain reading does not inspire
confidence.
4. We notice that initially a Division Bench of the High
Court of Bombay had stayed the proceedings, finding on a
perusal of the records that prima facie the complaint lodged
by the mother has no substance.  It was also specifically
noticed that the statement of the victim boy recorded under
Section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code by the learned
Page 2 of 5

--- Page 344 ---
Judicial Magistrate of the First Class indicates that no assault
as stated by the de-facto complainant had been occasioned. 
5. However, at the final hearing, despite their attention
being drawn to the said order, which is also referred to, the
learned Judges of the Division Bench without looking into the
FIS  or  the Section  164 statement, found that since cross
complaints are raised and there are accusations leveled, the
appellant must undergo trial. The learned Judges too had
observed that they were startled by the allegations made,
but failed to look at the material on record; which another
Division Bench had verified and found the complaint itself to
be  without  any  substance  for  reason  of  the  boy  having
stated no such incident before the Magistrate. 
6. The Division Bench which considered the matter ideally,
ought  to  have  looked  into  the  records  especially  when
another Division Bench; though in an interim order, noticed
that prima facie the allegations cannot stand. In the totality
of the circumstances, we are of the opinion that there is
absolutely no reason why the petitioner should be subjected
to a trial and the 2 nd respondent – the mother, has also not
entered appearance despite service having been effected.
Page 3 of 5

--- Page 345 ---
7. We hence quash FIR No.100/2024 registered at Khadki
Police Station, Pune under Section 354 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1908 and Section 8 of the Protection of Children from
Sexual  Offences  (POCSO)  Act,  2012.  There  shall  be  no
further proceedings taken in pursuance of the FIR.
8. The appeal stands allowed.  
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and learned
counsel for the respondent-State.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by Order dated 05.02.2025, passed by
the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur (briefly the ‘High
Court’ hereinafter) rejecting the regular bail application of the
appellant. Be it stated that appellant is an accused in Crime
No.364/2024, registered at Police Station Gandhi Nagar, District
Surguja, under Section 22(C) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic
Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985.
4. Allegation against the appellant is that 1500 injections of
Rexogesic Buprenorphine Injection ip 2 ml and 1500 injections of
Pheniramine Injection ip 10 ml , were seized from the possession of
the appellant for which appellant failed to give any proper
explanation.
1

--- Page 348 ---
5. By the impugned order, the High Court rejected the prayer for
bail of the appellant.
6. This Court  vide  order dated 09.06.2026, had issued notice
pursuant to which State has filed affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that appellant is in
custody since 17.06.2024, for more than 2 years now. He submits
that the recovery was made from a car allegedly driven by the
appellant not from the person of the appellant. Considering the
period of detention undergone, he prays that appellant may be
enlarged on bail.
8. Learned State counsel on the other hand has referred to
paragraph 9 (II) of the counter affidavit to submit that appellant
has 1 criminal antecedent of similar nature. Therefore, he may not
be enlarged on bail.
9. In response, learned counsel for the appellant submits that
the learned District & Sessions Judge, Distict- Gadwa, vide order
dated 21.01.2025, had enlarged the appellant on bail in the
connected NDPS Case No.12/2024.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and from a
perusal of the materials on record, we find that investigation has
not only been completed in this case, charges have also been framed
and trial has commenced. As on today, 9 out of 22 witnesses have
been examined. Appellant is in custody for more than 2 years now.
Examination  of  the  remaining  witnesses  may  take  some  time.
Therefore, an early conclusion of the trial does not seem a
possibility.
11. In such circumstances, we allow the present appeal by setting
2

--- Page 349 ---
aside the impugned order of the High Court dated 05.02.2025. We,
therefore, direct that the appellant shall be produced before the
concerned Special Judge within a maximum period of 7 days from
today, who shall thereafter enlarge the appellant on bail on such
terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
12. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

ITEM NO.25               COURT NO.5               SECTION II-D
               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition(s) for Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.) No(s).12827/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 12-05-2026
in SBCRMP No. 8757/2024 passed by the High Court of Judicature for
Rajasthan at Jaipur]
VIVEK JOSHI                                        Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS.                          Respondent(s)
FOR ADMISSION 
IA No. 203042/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 24-07-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Anand Mishra, AOR
                   
                  
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner is aggrieved with the impugned order of the
High Court which directed a chargesheet to be filed against the
absconding accused for offences under Sections 406 and 420 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) before the jurisdictional Court which
was also directed to proceed under Section 299 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.PC). The petitioner’s contention is
that though initially the FIR was lodged under Sections 406 and 420
IPC, he had omitted to include Section 66D of the Information and
Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act) which is also attracted on the

--- Page 352 ---
SLP (Crl.) No.12827/2026
allegations levelled. By an application, the same was sought to be
included which was allowed by the Judicial Magistrate No.7, Jaipur
Metropolitan-II.  The  omission  to  mention  Section  66D  in  the
impugned order prejudices the petitioner, is the contention. 
2. On a reading of the order of the High Court, it is very
evident that the High Court interacted with the Investigating
Officer  (I.O.)  who  was  present  in  person.  It  is  on  the
Investigation Officer’s submissions that she has prima facie found
the allegations under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC, that the
directions were issued. 
3. In fact, ideally the High Court ought to have only directed
the investigation to be concluded and chargesheet to be filed.
Abhinandan Jha  v. Dinesh Mishra 1, held that the formation of an
opinion, as to whether or not there is a case to place the accused
on trial, is exclusively that of the officer in-charge of the
investigation. 
4. In any event, we see that the impugned order only directs the
chargesheet to be filed under Sections 406 and 420 IPC, on the
submissions made by the I.O. before Court that such offences have
been made out. However, the cited decision also held that when a
chargesheet is filed before the Magistrate, it is the judicial
discretion of the Magistrate to take cognizance. Ram Naresh Prasad
v. State of Jharkhand & Ors. 2 held that even when a “Closure
Report”, finding no case made out is filed, the Court, though
cannot direct a chargesheet to be filed but could always take
1 1967 SCC OnLine SC 107
2 (2009) 11 SCC 299

--- Page 353 ---
SLP (Crl.) No.12827/2026
cognizance on the basis of the material in the report or direct
further investigation. 
5. H.S. Bains v. State (Union Territory of Chandigarh) 3 and
Ramswarup Soni v. State of Madhya Pradesh 4, reiterated that when a
Closure Report is filed, finding no offence made out, the Court has
three options; (i) to accept the same and close the proceedings or
(ii) take cognizance of the matter on the materials in the report
or (iii) direct further investigation.
6. Hence, even if the chargesheet is filed only under Section 406
and 420 IPC, it would be open for the Magistrate to decide whether
Section 66D has to be included or not, at the time of taking
cognizance.  The  petitioner  would  be  entitled  to  urge  his
contentions at that point. 
7. Insofar as the direction to file the chargesheet under Section
299; the provision speaks of recording of evidence in the absence
of accused. It is in the circumstances of the accused having
absconded that the High Court made mention of Section 299, only
reminding  the  Magistrate’s  Court  that  when  an  accused  is
absconding, if there is no chance of the accused being apprehended,
then the evidence should be recorded which would be used against
the accused on his apprehension later, if the witnesses are not
available or cannot be procured at that point of time.   
8. We find no reason to interfere with the order passed by the
High Court but only clarify that the Magistrate would have the
discretion to consider whether cognizance is to be taken under
3 (1980) 4 SCC 631
4 2019 SCC OnLine 1335

--- Page 354 ---
SLP (Crl.) No.12827/2026
Section 66D of the IT Act at the time the same is considered by the
Magistrate. So far as Section 299, it is the call of the Magistrate
to decide whether the facts of the case require the invocation of
Section 299 of Cr.PC. 
9. With the above reservations, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
 
(HARPREET KAUR)                                (POOJA SHARMA)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

                            VERSUS

     O R D E R
1. The appellant is aggrieved by the
order passed by the Division Bench of the
High  Court  of  judicature  at  Madras
dismissing  his  appeal  on  the  ground  of
availability of alternative remedy.
2. Appellant’s Writ Petition, bearing
W.P. No. 23950 of 2006, was also dismissed
on the ground that the appellant had an
effective and efficacious remedy in the form
of filing an appeal against the order sought
to be assailed in the Writ Petition. The
said order was passed  upholding the order
passed  by  the  Assessing  Officer  on
05.05.2006  imposing  sales  tax  on  the
appellant for the establishment of diesel
generators.

--- Page 376 ---
2
3. Learned counsel appearing for the
appellant would submit that the appellant’s
case relates to Assessment Year 2003-2004.
Therefore,  even  under  the  second  Kone
Elevators judgment,  i.e.,  Kone  Elevator
India Pvt. Ltd.  vs.  State of Tamil Nadu,
(2014) 7 SCC 1, for transactions prior to
the Amending Act which came into force on
01.04.2007, the appellant’s case should be
considered in light of the order passed by
this Court in the W.P.(C) Nos. 66-67/2012,
and this Court may pass a similar order as
was passed in the W.P.(C) Nos. 66-67/2012.
4. Considering  the  order  passed  by
this Court in W.P.(C) No. 66-67/2012, we
dispose of this civil appeal by directing
the Assessing Officer to undertake fresh
assessment or reassessment, as the case may
be,  in view of the law laid down by this
Court  in  Kone  Elevator  India  Pvt.  Ltd.
(supra).
5. The  appeal  stands  disposed  of
accordingly.

1
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
   CIVIL APPEAL NO.          OF 2026
    (Arising out of SLP(C) No.33148 of 2025)
SHABEER                              APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
ARUNDAS                              RESPONDENT
O R D E R
Heard learned counsels for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  present  appeal  challenges  the  impugned  order  dated
29.10.2025 passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Kerala
at Ernakulam in RCREV. No.112 of 2025 by which, the order passed by
the Rent Control Court on 31.07.2023 in R.C.P. No.17 of 2022 and as
upheld by the Rent Control Appellate Authority on 05.03.2025 in
R.C.A. No.107 of 2023 under Section 12(3) of the Kerala Buildings
(Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 for eviction of the respondent
on the ground of default in payment of rent, has been set aside.
4. The Rent Control Court ruled in favour of the appellant-
landlord and directed for eviction of the respondent-tenant. The
same  was  upheld  in  challenge  by  the  Rent  Control  Appellate
Authority. Further challenge to the same before the High Court
succeeded in favour of the respondent-tenant vide the impugned
order.
5. Learned counsel for the appellant-landlord submitted that the

--- Page 380 ---
2
ground for eviction was non-payment of rent by the respondent-
tenant for a long period of time. Such contention had been upheld
by the Rent Control Court as well as by the Rent Control Appellate
Authority and even the High Court has not disputed the same.
However, on an issue which was non-existent and ought not to have
been raised as a bogey before the High Court, specifically relating
to challenge to the title of the appellant, the matter has been
remanded for fresh consideration to the Rent Control Court. Learned
counsel for the appellant-landlord drew the attention of the Court
to a specific finding of the Rent Control Court where it is noted
that in the response filed by the respondent-tenant, there was no
denial of title of the appellant-landlord. This finding has not
been controverted by the respondent-tenant and only today, orally,
it has been submitted that the title was disputed for the period
for which, the entire rent was said to be in default and it is only
later that the appellant-landlord became the owner by way of
purchase of the suit property.
6. Learned counsel for the respondent-tenant submitted that the
respondent had genuine cause to contest the matter as at the
relevant point of time, someone else was the owner of the building
and default for that period, cannot be pursued by the appellant. It
was further submitted that the High Court had only remanded the
matter for fresh consideration to the Rent Control Court on the
point of title which should not be interfered with as the appellant
shall  have  full  opportunity  to  canvass  whatever  points  are
available to him, both on facts as well as in law.
7. Having considered the matter in its entirety, we record at the

--- Page 381 ---
3
outset, that the impugned order passed by the Division Bench of the
High  Court  cannot  be  sustained  on  the  short  point  that  in
revisional jurisdiction, the issue which was never in contest
between the parties has been given primacy and has been directed to
be reconsidered by the First Court (Rent Control Court). The issue
of title changes the entire nature of litigation between the
parties and at the final stage before the High Court, it ought not
to have been even considered much less, in view of the admission by
the respondent-tenant with regard to the title of the appellant-
landlord that too, in a formal written objection filed before the
Rent Control Court.
8. Accordingly, for the reason aforesaid, the appeal succeeds and
is allowed. The impugned order dated 29.10.2025 passed by the
Division Bench of the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam in RCREV.
No.112 of 2025 stands set aside and order dated 05.03.2025 passed
by the Rent Control Appellate Authority in R.C.A. No.107 of 2023
upholding the order passed by the Rent Control Court on 31.07.2023
in R.C.P. No.17 of 2022 stands restored. No order as to costs.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
      ……………………………………………………………………J.
       [AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH]
…………………………………………………………………………J.
                   [MANMOHAN]
NEW DELHI
22nd JULY, 2026

BHANDARI SCRAP TRADERS                             Petitioner(s)

WITH

(FOR ADMISSION)

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Though we are informed that a special leave petition has been
entertained in relation to the decision of the Tripura High Court
1

--- Page 388 ---
SLP(C) No. 23931/2026 etc.
in Sahil Enterprises vs. Union of India & Ors. 1, we find from the
judgment passed by the High Court of Tripura that the exercise
undertaken by the High Court of Gujarat in the judgment, presently
under challenge, was not undertaken by it.  
The distinction and differences between the provisions of the
Delhi Value Added Tax Act, 2004 2, and the Central Goods and
Services Tax Act, 2017 3, brought out by way of a detailed analysis
from paragraph 42 onwards in the impugned judgment along with the
scheme of availing Input Tax Credit (ITC) under the GST regime, as
set  out  in  paragraph  56  of  the  impugned  judgment,  clearly
demonstrate that there is no possibility of drawing parity between
the provisions of the two enactments, so as to treat a purchasing
dealer under the CGST Act on par with a purported bonafide
purchasing dealer under the Delhi VAT Act in relation to ITC, when
the supplier-dealer fails to pay the requisite tax.
Further, the High Court of Gujarat has also referred to the
provisions of Section 41 of the CGST Act and also Sections 73 and
74 thereof in the context of the purchasing dealer under the CGST
regime being entitled to re-avail the reversed ITC after the
supplier-dealer is made to discharge the tax liability.
In that view of the matter, the High Court was fully justified
in holding that no grounds were made out to declare Section 16(2)
(c) of the CGST Act as unconstitutional or read down the provisions
1 [(2026) 154 GSTR 108 (Tri.)]
2  “Delhi VAT Act”, for short
3  “CGST Act”, for short
2

--- Page 389 ---
SLP(C) No. 23931/2026 etc.
thereof.  We find ourselves in complete and respectful agreement
with the views expressed by the High Court of Gujarat and affirm
and uphold the impugned judgment.
The special leave petitions are, accordingly, dismissed.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(DEEPAK GUGLANI)                             (PREETI SAXENA)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                         COURT MASTER (NSH)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s).  320 OF 2013  
BASIR                                              APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
STATE(GOVT.OF NCT OF DELHI)                        RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The appellant challenges the judgment/order dated
01.02.2010 passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
in Criminal Appeal No.630 of 2005.
2.  We  have  heard  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respective parties and perused the material available on
record.
3. Concurrently, the Courts below convicted the accused-
appellant herein for committing the offence punishable
under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced
him to suffer imprisonment for life and also to pay a
fine of Rs.5,000/- (Rupees five thousand only) with a
default clause.
4. It is not in dispute that the appellant and the
deceased were husband and wife. The deceased was found
dead in the house of the accused in the morning of
18.07.2003.  It  has  come  in  the  testimony  of  the
appellant’s daughter born out of the wedlock, i.e., PW5,
that on the previous night the entire family, that is,
the  accused,  the  deceased  wife,  and  the  two  (02)
1

--- Page 406 ---
children, had gone to sleep, and in the middle of the
night, when she woke up hearing the cries of her mother,
she found her father to be missing. In fact, she saw him
leaving the bedroom. The accused has not furnished any
explanation as is mandated under law.
5. The testimony of PW5 to the effect that the accused
was seen fleeing away from the spot immediately after the
occurrence of the incident stands corroborated by the
neighbour-PW4.
6. As such, we find no merit in the appeal, and the same
stands dismissed.
7. Needless to add, it is the appellant’s right to seek
the benefit of the policy of remission in accordance with
law.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 82 OF 2011 
 
 
STATE OF RAJASTHAN                              APPELLANT(S) 
 
 
                                VERSUS 
 
 
SABIR KHAN                                      RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
 
 
1. This appeal, preferred by the State of Rajasthan, is 
directed against the judgment and order dated 07.04.2010 passed 
by the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jodhpur in 
D.B. Criminal Appeal No. 1184 of 2003. By the impugned 
judgment, the High Court partly interfered with the conviction 
recorded by the Trial Court, modifying it from Section 302 IPC 
to Section 304 Part I IPC. 
2. Vide judgment dated 18.10.2003, the learned Sessions Judge 
(Fast Track Court), Pali, convicted the respondent under 
Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to imprisonment for life with 
fine of ₹2000/-. He was further convicted under Sections 25 and 
27 of the Arms Act, with sentences of two years RI and three 
years RI respectively, along with fines of ₹1000/ - each. All 
sentences were directed to run concurrently. 
 

--- Page 409 ---
2 
3. On appeal, the High Court re -appreciated the evidence and 
altered the conviction to Section 304 Part I IPC, sentencing 
the respondent to nine years rigorous imprisonment and fine of 
₹5000/-, while maintaining the convictions under the Arms Act. 
Quite apparently, there was no interference with the conviction  
of the later. 
4. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and 
perused the material on record. In our considered view, the 
High Court did not commit any error in reading, appreciating or 
evaluating the evidence ; also correctly  interpreting the 
relevant statutory provisions.  
5. The medical evidence, specifically the testimony of PW -4 
Dr. A.K. Naval, who conducted the autopsy, establishes that the 
deceased, Shahjad Khan (referred to as Sajid Khan in the 
submissions), died as a result of gunshot injuries to vital 
organs, namely the heart and lungs. 
6. A perusal of the testimony of the eyewitnesses, including 
PW-1 (Peeru Khan), PW -2 (Smt. Pyari), and PW -3 (Pappu alias 
Ramjan), who were declared hostile by the prosecution, 
indicates that the occurrence took place during a scuffle where 
both the deceased and the accused were armed. The nature of the 
incident does not suggest premeditation or a calculated 
endeavour to take revenge due to previous animosity; rather, it 
appears to have been a sudden fight occurring in the heat of 
passion. The prosecution ca se, therefore, primarily rested on 
PW-13 (Nasir Khan, father of the deceased), PW -14 (Smt. 
Rashida, mother), and PW-15 (Parvez Khan, brother), who arrived 

--- Page 410 ---
3 
at the spot immediately after hearing the gunfire and saw the 
respondent fleeing while carrying a firearm. Their testimonies, 
along with the corroboration by PW -16 (Shakkur) regarding the 
inspection of the site, support the sequence of events 
immediately following the incident. 
7. The evidence thus indicates that both the deceased and 
accused were armed; after a scuffle, the accused fired the gun. 
The nature of the occurrence was not one of premeditation or 
deliberate revenge for past animosity. It was a sudden fight in 
the heat of passion, without the accused taking undue advantage 
or acting in a cruel or unusual manner. 
8. For the reasons stated above, we find no ground to 
interfere with the well -reasoned judgment of the High Court. 
Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. Pending application(s), 
if any, shall stand disposed of. 
 
 
        ........................J. 
                   (SANJAY KAROL) 
 
 
 
 
         ...........................J.  
                                    (AUGUSTINE GEORGE MASIH)     
 
NEW DELHI; 
JULY 22, 2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.7006/2016
SHIV NATH SHARMA             APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR & ORS.                RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. This civil appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 07 th
April, 2016 of the High Court of Judicature at Patna dismissing the appellant’s
intra-court appeal1 with costs. The appeal arose out of an order dated 18 th May,
2015 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court dismissing the appellant’s writ
petition2.  
2. The dispute is in relation to the date of birth of the appellant.
3. The matriculation examination, which the appellant qualified in the year
1971, led to the issuance of a certificate (page 16 of the paper book) showing
his date of birth as 05 th June, 1952, whereas the Uttar Madhyama examination
(page 14 of the paper book), allegedly taken by the appellant in 1970, records
his date of birth as 05th June, 1955. 
4. The  date  of  birth  of  the  appellant,  as  evident  from  the  matriculation
certificate, was inserted in the service records which he disputed after long
years of service.
1 LPA No.1527 of 2015
2 Civil Writ Jurisdiction Case No.4494 of 2015
1

--- Page 430 ---
5. We are at a loss to comprehend as to how the appellant could qualify the
Class  XII  examination  in  1970,  before  he  qualified  in  the  matriculation
examination of 1971. 
6. Be that as it may, we are of the considered opinion that the High Court
was absolutely justified in not entertaining the writ petition as well as the intra-
court appeal. 
7. We also record that this is a matter, where no leave ought to have been
granted in the first place. 
8. Having regard to the facts and circumstance noted above, the civil appeal
is dismissed.
9. Time to pay costs of Rs.10,000/- (Rupees ten thousand) only in terms of
the impugned order dated 07th April, 2016 is extended by a month from date.
10. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

(DIPANKAR DATTA)
...........................................J.
(SHEEL NAGU)

Code  of  Civil  Procedure,  1908  of  the  appellant-Haryana  State  Agricultural
Marketing Board3.
2. It appears on a reading of the impugned judgment that the suit instituted
by  the  respondent  was  decreed,  whereupon  a  first  appeal  carried  by  the
appellant-Board from such decree was also dismissed.
3. In dismissing the second appeal, the learned Judge of the High Court
relied on an earlier decision dated 21 st May, 2009 of the High Court in R.S.A-

1 High Court

3 Appellant-Board
1

the order passed by the High Court dated 21 st May, 2009 in R.S.A-1622-2008
has duly been implemented.

1. Leave granted.

FIR No. 186 of 2025 for the offences punishable under
Sections 21(c),22(b) and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 111 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and for the offences pun-
ishable under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and  
Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999  (for
short, “the MCOCA Act”).
3. The appellant preferred an appeal under Section 12
of the MCOCA Act, before the High Court of Delhi, as -
sailing the order dated 31.10.2025 passed by the Ses -
sions Court, whereby her bail application was rejected.
The High Court also dismissed the said appeal. Ag -
grieved thereby, the appellant is before us.
1

--- Page 442 ---
4. The sum and substance of the case against the appel-
lant is that she, along with her family members, was
running a drug syndicate and facilitating the traffick-
ing and concealment of narcotic substances.
5. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the appellant and the learned ASG appearing for the
respondent-State.
6. Taking note of the period of incarceration already
undergone by the appellant, the fact that she is a
woman, and the fact that the contraband involved is of
intermediate quantity, we are inclined to set aside the
impugned order passed by the High Court and grant her
bail.  Accordingly, the appellant is directed to be re-
leased on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
imposed by the concerned Trial Court.

STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH & ORS.                   Petitioner(s)

RAMESH CHAND                                       Respondent(s)
FOR ADMISSION 
 
Date : 24-07-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Ketan Paul, AOR
                   Mr. Prachet Sharma, Adv.
                   Ms. Ujala Singh, Adv.
                   
                   
For Respondent(s)  
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Learned counsel for the petitioner(s) submits that while
directing the respondent's regularization on the basis of
Mool Raj Upadhyaya vs. State of Himachal Pradesh [1994 Supp.
(2) SCC 316], the learned Single Judge has observed that the
respondent is entitled to regularization upon completing 10
years of service as a daily wager, whereas Mool Raj ( supra)
had not issued any such direction. 
2. In Mool Raj ( supra), this Court had issued the following
directions:
1

--- Page 451 ---
“4. Taking into consideration the facts and
circumstances of the case, we modify the said
scheme by substituting paragraphs 1 to 4 of the
same by the following paragraphs:
(1) Daily-wage/muster-roll workers, whether
skilled or unskilled, who have completed 10
years or more of continuous service with a
minimum of 240 days in a calendar year on
31-12-1993, shall be appointed as work-
charged employees with effect from 1-1-1994
and shall be put in the time-scale of pay
applicable  to  the  corresponding  lowest
grade in the Government;
(2) daily-wage/muster-roll workers, whether
skilled  or  unskilled,  who  have  not
completed 10 years of continuous service
with a minimum of 240 days in a calendar
year on 31-12-1993, shall be appointed as
work-charged employees with effect from the
date they complete the said period of 10
years of service and on such appointment
they shall be put in the time-scale of pay
applicable  to  the  lowest  grade  in  the
Government;
(3) daily-wage/muster-roll workers, whether
skilled or unskilled who have not completed
10 years of service with a minimum of 240
days in a calendar year on 31-12-1993,
shall be paid daily wages at the rates
prescribed by the Government of Himachal
Pradesh from time to time for daily-wage
employees falling in Class III and Class IV
till they are appointed as work-charged
employees in accordance with paragraph 2;
(4) daily-wage/muster-roll workers shall be
regularised in a phased manner on the basis
of  seniority-cum-suitability  including
physical fitness. On regularisation they
shall be put in the minimum of the time-
scale payable to the corresponding lowest
grade  applicable  to  the  Government  and
would be entitled to all other benefits
2

--- Page 452 ---
available to regular government servants of
the corresponding grade.”
3. In view of the above, we feel that the observation made by
the learned Single Judge that the respondent is entitled to
regularization immediately upon completion of 10 years of
service as a daily wager—may not be correct.
4. However, since the respondent has been in service as a
cook since 1996 i.e for nearly 30 years, we are not inclined
to entertain this Special Leave Petition.
5. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition is dismissed,
however, the order passed by the learned Single Judge,
against which the petitioner's intra-court appeal has been
dismissed by the Division Bench of the High Court on the
ground of delay, shall not be a precedent.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
(MINI)                                  (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL) NO.6765/2026]
NANDINI V.                            Appellant(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF KARNATAKA & ORS.            Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, who is the wife of the detenue, has
preferred the present appeal, being aggrieved by
the dismissal of the writ petition by the High
Court,  seeking  setting  aside  of  the  detention
order passed against the detenue. 
3. Learned counsel for the appellant raised only one
issue, as recorded by this Court while issuing
notice, that there is a clear non-application of
mind  with  respect  to  the  antecedents  of  the
appellant. While the appellant’s conviction was
modified to the offence punishable under Part II
of Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(‘IPC’), it was noted that he was convicted under
Section 302 of the IPC.
1

--- Page 463 ---
4. While not disputing the aforesaid error, learned
counsel for the State submitted that this should
not enure to the benefit of the appellant. 
5. This is a case of clear non-application of mind.
The facts have been wrongly recorded, and the
detaining authority, if not for the same, perhaps
would not have passed the detention order.
6. Considering the above, we are inclined to set
aside the order of detention as well as the order
of the High Court.
7. The Appeal stands allowed.
8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
. . . . . . . . .,J
[M.M. SUNDRESH]  
. . . . . . . . . . . ,J
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]

       UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
SLP(Crl) No. 17662/2025
We find that one of the petitioners in this case, viz. Barun
Kumar Choudhary, is clearly guilty of abuse of process. It is seen
from the List of Dates in this special leave petition filed on
08.10.2025 that a specific reference was made to the High Court’s
order  dated  25.04.2025.  Conveniently,  no  mention  was  made
thereafter of the fact that SLP(Crl.) No. 12190/2025 was filed by
Barun Kumar Choudhary and others, and the said special leave
petition was dismissed on 18.08.2025, that is long before the
institution of this special leave petition on 08.10.2025.  
The non-disclosure of this relevant fact demonstrates manifest
lack of bonafides on the part of Barun Kumar Choudhary, which would
be equally applicable to the other petitioners in the special leave
petition, as they chose to join hands with him.
The special leave petition is, accordingly, dismissed on this
short ground.

CIVIL APPEAL NO.8994/2026

OCASA DESIGN STUDIO PVT LTD RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The National Disputes Redressal Commission 1, New Delhi, was
not justified in opining that it did not have the power and
the wherewithal to determine the alleged deficiency in service
by undertaking the recording of evidence and by permitting
cross-examination  of  witnesses  apart  from  evaluation  of
architectural drawings, quality and quantity of specialized
equipment and specialist works services. The conclusion drawn
to the effect that such evaluation was not feasible in
proceedings before the NCDRC, is, therefore, incorrect. 
2. However, we may also note that the appellant filed its counter
claim before the Arbitral Tribunal and the learned counsel
appearing for the appellant fairly admitted before the NCDRC
that the said counter claim would have a bearing on the
consumer complaint. 
3. That being so, we find no grounds to interfere with the
1  “NCDRC”, for short
1

--- Page 484 ---
impugned direction of the NCDRC leaving it open to the
appellant  and  the  respondent  to  take  appropriate  legal
recourse towards their grievances, if warranted. The appellant
is, therefore, not remediless.
4. The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed.

               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C) No.29190/2024
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 27-08-2024 
in WA No. 100006/2022 passed by the High Court of Karnataka Circuit
Bench at Dharwad]
PASCHIM VIBHAG SHIKSHANA MANDAL                       Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
THE PASCHIM VIBHAG SHIKSHANA MANDAL & ANR.            Respondent(s)
IA No. 91064/2025 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
IA No. 91063/2025 - PERMISSION TO FILE ADDITIONAL 
DOCUMENTS/FACTS/ANNEXURES
IA No. 51127/2025 - PERMISSION TO FILE ADDITIONAL 
DOCUMENTS/FACTS/ANNEXURES
 
Date : 21-07-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE M.M. SUNDRESH
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE PRASANNA B. VARALE
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Anand Sanjay M Nuli, Sr. Adv.
                   M/S.  Nuli & Nuli, AOR
                   Ms. Akhila Wali, Adv.
                   Mr. Abhishekh Singh, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Gagan Gupta, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Anuj Udupa, Adv.
                   Mr. Akshay Amritanshu, AOR
                   Mr. Sarthak Srivastava, Adv.
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned Senior counsel appearing for
the petitioner as well as for the respondent.
2. The present Special Leave Petition is nothing but a
dispute between two groups. While one group seeks to
uphold the change in status to that of a Society, the
other seeks to continue as a Trust. It would be sufficient
1

--- Page 526 ---
to observe that, as of now, the Society has come into
existence. 
3. On  a  perusal  of  the  impugned  judgment  of  the
Division Bench, we find that the directions issued with
respect to the use of the same name, and the consequential
administrative  action  entrusted  to  the  statutory
authority,  cannot  be  sustained  in  the  eye  of  law,
especially when the Division Bench itself has observed
that  these  issues  will  have  to  be  adjudicated  in
accordance with the provisions of the Act.
4. In our considered view, the principal question that
falls  for  consideration  is  to  the  validity  of  the
resolution that led to the registration of the Society.
Suffice it to say that, as of now, the Society has been
formed.
5. In said view of the matter, we are inclined to set
aside the judgment of the Division Bench with respect to
the finding that the Trust and the Society can use the
same  name  as  well  as  the  observations  conferring
jurisdiction upon the statutory authority. The parties are
at liberty to file their respective suit in respect of all
other issues before the jurisdictional Court within a
period of six weeks from the date of receipt of a copy of
this order.
6. Inasmuch as we have held that the parties are at
liberty to avail themselves of the civil remedy, any
observations made by the Division Bench shall not stand in
2

--- Page 527 ---
the way of the Civil Court on considering the issues
afresh.
7. The  Special  Leave  Petition  is  disposed  of,
accordingly.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
 (KRITIKA TIWARI)                                 (POONAM VAID)
 COURT MASTER (SH)                             ASSISTANT REGISTRAR
3

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Amrendra Kumar Mehta, learned counsel for the
petitioner and Mr. Raj Karan Singh Verka, learned counsel for
the respondent nos.1, 2 & 4 to 7 - respondents/land owners.
2. The present petition filed by the National Highways
Authority of India calls in question the correctness of the
interim order dated  15-10-2024 in FAO No. 4688/2023 (O&M)
passed by the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh. By
the said interim order, the High Court, while directing the
petitioner herein to deposit the entire compensation amount as

--- Page 634 ---
2
awarded by the Arbitrator within a period of two months,
provided a mechanism for withdrawal. Under the said mechanism,
it was directed that 50% of the amount has to be disbursed to
the  land-owner(s)  against  the  adequate  security  to  the
satisfaction of the Executing Court concerned and the balance
amount be kept in a fixed deposit so that it earns the maximum
interest.
3. Having considered the facts and circumstances, on the
peculiar facts, we are satisfied that the impugned order
serves the ends of justice.
4. We find no good ground to interfere with the impugned
judgment/order(s). The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly,
dismissed.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(NIRMALA NEGI)                                  (MANOJ KUMAR)

Mr. Kamal Rattan Digpaul, Adv. 
Mr. S.N. Terdal, Adv. 
Mr. Piyush Beriwal, Adv. 
        UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
As the petitioner, Amit Shukla, surrendered on 08.06.2026
pursuant to the order dated 27.04.2026 passed by a learned Judge
in-Chambers, we find no reason to pass further orders in this
special leave petition. 
1

--- Page 884 ---
However, we find that the Certificate of Imprisonment issued
by the Deputy Superintendent, Central Jail No. 2, Tihar Jail, New
Delhi, records that the petitioner had to surrender on 01.06.2026,
but he failed to do so on the due date and only surrendered 7 days
later, that is, on 08.06.2026.
We may note that the aforestated statement is incorrect, as
the six weeks’ time granted by this Court, vide the order dated
27.04.2026, expired on 08.06.2026 and not on 01.06.2026, as noted
by Deputy Superintendent. 
Even if it can be understood otherwise, we make it clear that
the time granted by this Court shall be deemed to have expired only
on 08.06.2026, the date on which the petitioner did surrender.  The
jail authorities shall make a note of the same and shall not treat
the petitioner as having committed any lapse in that regard. 
Subject to the above observation, the special leave petition
is dismissed.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
(BABITA PANDEY)                              (PREETI SAXENA)

was held guilty by the Trial Court for the alleged crime and was
sentenced to undergo life imprisonment with fine. The Appeal
preferred by the petitioner before the High Court also failed. In
such circumstances, the petitioner is here before us with the
present petition.

--- Page 896 ---
2
3. We heard the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner
- convict as well as the learned counsel appearing for the
State.
4. We are of the view that no error not to speak of any
error of law could be said to have been committed by the High
Court in passing the impugned Judgment and Order.
5. However, we take notice of the fact that the petitioner
is undergoing sentence of life imprisonment past 16 years.
6. In such circumstances, referred to above, we direct the
State to place on record the following:
(i) Report of the jail authorities as regards the
overall conduct of the petitioner;
(ii) The  whereabouts   and  the  family  status  of  
the victim;
(iii)  The remission   policy  of  the  State Government
prevailing  as  on   date  of  the  commission  of the
offence  or  any  other  remission   policy  which  is
more   beneficial  to    the petitioner as on date.
